title: How six animals sleep: sea otters, koalas, dolphins, horses, bats and frigatebirds

facts.text: Sea otters usually rest in groups and wrap themselves in kelp or seagrass so they do not drift while resting.
A resting sea otter lies on its back in the water, and kelp across its body keeps it from drifting out to sea.
Koalas eat mainly eucalyptus leaves, which are low in energy and hard to break down.
Koalas can sleep up to 20 hours a day because of their low-energy diet.
Koalas often rest high up in a fork of a gum (eucalyptus) tree.
Dolphins sleep with one half of the brain at a time while the other half stays awake; the eye on the awake side can stay open.
Dolphins breathe air and must come up to the surface to breathe, even while resting.
Horses can lock the main joints of their legs, so they can stand and doze with very little muscle effort.
Horses must lie down to get REM sleep, the deepest stage of sleep.
Because horses are prey animals, they lie down only when they feel comfortable and safe.
Bats rest upside down in high places; tendons lock their toes, and their body weight keeps them hanging without using much energy.
Great frigatebirds can spend weeks flying non-stop over the ocean.
Frigatebirds can sleep while flying, with one brain half or both halves asleep at once.
In flight, frigatebirds slept only about 42 minutes a day; on land they slept more than 12 hours a day.
